The input 𝐬 \mathbf{s} is assumed to be an anatomically plausible semantic label map. It must be represented in polar coordinates at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution and encoded using the same discrete anatomical-label convention and color mapping used during training. Such masks may come from reusable anatomical templates, atlas-based models, manually edited cases, procedurally generated anatomies, or deformed versions of existing labeled anatomies. To generate controlled dynamic or pathological scenarios, a user-defined transformation t t can be applied to the input label map before image synthesis, yielding 𝐬 ~ = t ⁡ ( 𝐬 ) \tilde{\mathbf{s}}=t(\mathbf{s}) . We simulated breathing-like motion by deforming the 3D semantic label volumes over eight temporal states using a simplified parametric displacement field. The deformation amplitude varied sinusoidally over time and was spatially modulated by a Gaussian profile to produce smooth, non-rigid motion concentrated toward the anterior side of the volume. Each anatomical label was warped independently using nearest-neighbor interpolation to preserve discrete label values, while the bone class was kept fixed as a rigid reference. This procedure provides a cyclic approximation of respiratory motion and should be interpreted as a simplified deformation model rather than a biomechanical simulation of abdominal breathing. Pathological scenarios were generated by manually editing the 2D semantic label maps in 3D Slicer. Pathological regions were introduced by modifying existing anatomical labels or adding new labeled regions while preserving the same color-coded semantic convention used during training. The edits were manually designed by the authors to create anatomically plausible proof-of-concept examples, rather than being randomly sampled or derived from a formal clinical protocol. In the experiments reported here, the starting masks were held-out anatomical label maps from the test set, which were used only as semantic inputs to the pipeline. The corresponding physics-based simulations were used only as references for Stage I evaluation. For pathological cases, examples of liver tumors, abdominal aortic aneurysms, kidney stones, and gallbladder polyps were generated as described in Section 3.2.2 . 2.5 Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis Evaluating generative image models is inherently challenging because no single metric can fully capture image fidelity, anatomical correctness, perceptual realism, and distributional similarity. This is particularly relevant in US simulation, where images contain stochastic speckle patterns and acoustic artifacts that may differ locally even when the underlying anatomy and clinically relevant appearance are correctly preserved. We therefore followed common practice in the US simulation literature and combined complementary metrics designed to assess different properties of the generated images Zhang et al. (2021) ; Tomar et al. (2021) ; Liang et al. (2022a) ; Katakis et al. (2023) ; Peng et al. (2025) ; Du et al. (2026) ; Domínguez et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2023) . For Stage I, simulated images were compared with their paired physics-based reference images 𝐱 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{x}} . The evaluation metrics were grouped into two complementary categories: (i) morphological and anatomical metrics, including Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and mean Intersection over Union (mIoU), which assess reconstruction fidelity and preservation of spatial and anatomical structure; and (ii) perceptual and distributional metrics, including Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and Kernel Inception Distance (KID), which assess feature-level similarity and agreement between image distributions. Intensity fidelity was quantified using MAE, MSE, and PSNR. These metrics measure pixel-wise differences between generated and reference images, with MAE and MSE directly quantifying reconstruction error and PSNR expressing this error relative to the available intensity range Zhang et al. (2021) ; Katakis et al. (2023) ; Peng et al. (2025) . Structural similarity was evaluated using SSIM, which compares local luminance, contrast, and structural patterns Zhang et al. (2021) ; Tomar et al. (2021) ; Chen et al. (2023) ; Peng et al. (2025) . Because pixel-wise similarity does not necessarily imply preservation of anatomical content, we also evaluated anatomical consistency using mIoU across 16 abdominal structures. The same segmentation model S S was applied to each physics-based reference image and its corresponding simulated image, and the resulting predictions were compared. The mIoU therefore measures whether anatomical structures detectable in the reference image remain consistently represented after image synthesis. As this evaluation depends on the robustness of S S on generated images, mIoU was interpreted as a relative measure of segmentation consistency rather than as an independent estimate of anatomical accuracy Zhang et al. (2023a) . Perceptual similarity was assessed using LPIPS, which measures discrepancies between deep feature representations and is less dependent on exact pixel correspondence Domínguez et al. (2024) ; Peng et al. (2025) . Distribution-level similarity was assessed using FID and KID. Unlike the preceding image-level metrics, FID and KID compare feature distributions extracted from the complete sets of reference and generated images rather than individual image pairs. FID is widely used to evaluate generative models, whereas KID provides an unbiased estimator that can be more appropriate for relatively small datasets. Although both metrics rely on an Inception v3 network pretrained on ImageNet and are therefore not specific to US, they have been used in previous US synthesis studies Liang et al. (2022b) ; Liang et al. (2022a) ; Tomar et al. (2021) ; Zhang et al. (2021) . Following previous work Tomar et al. (2021) , features were extracted from the intermediate 768-dimensional layer to reduce reliance on the final, ImageNet-specific representation. FID and KID were computed using the TorchFidelity package Obukhov et al. (2020) . Stage II was evaluated here primarily as a downstream compatibility test, to determine whether the images generated by the proposed Stage I models produce refined outputs comparable to those obtained when the same refinement module is applied to physics-based ray-casting images. Stage II could not be evaluated using paired reconstruction metrics because no corresponding real US image was available for each refined image. Its evaluation therefore focused on similarity to the real US domain. Global distributional similarity was quantified using FID and KID, while organ-specific echogenicity was evaluated using χ 2 \chi^{2} distances between intensity histograms extracted from selected anatomical regions. Lower histogram distances indicate greater agreement between the intensity distributions of generated and real tissues. Because these quantitative measures do not directly capture ultrasound-specific artifact correctness or clinical plausibility, they were interpreted together with anatomy-aware consistency measures and qualitative inspection of relevant acoustic phenomena, including acoustic shadows, anechoic regions, and hyperechoic responses. For the statistical analysis of Stage I, MAE, MSE, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and mIoU were computed independently for each test image. Pix2Pix and SDM were therefore compared using paired vectors containing one observation per image. Differences between methods were assessed using one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with statistical significance defined as p < 0.05 p<0.05 . FID and KID were treated as dataset-level metrics because each value summarizes the complete reference and generated image distributions. Consequently, they were not subjected to image-level hypothesis testing. Instead, their uncertainty was estimated using 95% bootstrap confidence intervals based on 1,000 resamples. The same bootstrap procedure was used for FID and KID in the Stage I and Stage II evaluations. 3 Results We evaluated each stage of the proposed pipeline both quantitatively and qualitatively.
